text: Last lesson, you learned subledgers raise business events and hand them to Subledger Accounting. This lesson gets specific: what exactly is an event, and what are event classes and event types, two terms you'll see constantly for the rest of this course.

An accounting event is a business occurrence that may require a journal entry. Validating an AP invoice, applying a receipt, adding a fixed asset - each is an event. Editing a supplier's address is not; only changes with potential financial impact qualify. And every event arrives as a structured package: what kind of event, which transaction, and the data SLA needs.

Oracle groups events into event classes - a category of transaction within a subledger, like Invoices in Payables. Within a class, specific event types describe exactly what happened: Invoice Validated, Invoice Adjusted, Invoice Cancelled. Rules are usually written at the class level, and refined at the type level when one situation needs different treatment.

Picture Payables validating a five thousand dollar invoice: event class Invoices, event type Invoice Validated. Later someone adjusts that invoice. Same event class, Invoices, but a different event type: Invoice Adjusted. Rules you'll build later can treat those two differently, because the event type says exactly what occurred.

Why classify at all? Without event classes and types, every rule would need its own conditional logic to figure out what kind of transaction it's looking at. Instead, Oracle gives you a stable, documented vocabulary. When you build account rules and journal line rules next chapter, you'll literally pick an event class and event type from a list.

So remember: an event is a business occurrence that may need a journal entry, classified by event class and event type. Up next, lesson three: accounting methods and rules, where this vocabulary gets attached to real journal-building logic.
